paper_design_summary: In a preregistered 2 x 3 between-subjects online experiment, 644 Prolific writers were analyzed (318 native English, L1; 326 non-native, L2). Each wrote four creative metaphors, each with a short explanation, without AI, with five GPT-4o candidate metaphors and explanations per scenario (AI ideation), or with five GPT-4o candidate explanations for a metaphor they wrote themselves (AI refinement). The paper does not say how writers were allocated to these conditions, and L2 writers in the AI arms chose English or their native language for the AI interaction. Collective diversity was scored as each metaphor's embedding cosine similarity to the leave-one-out centroid of the other metaphors for the same scenario in the same condition, and 351 blinded Prolific evaluators rated novelty, surprise, appropriateness, and explanation quality. A second, non-preregistered study simulated the writer pool with persona-prompted LLMs (GPT-4o mini, Claude Sonnet 4.6, Qwen3.5-27b) and compared simulated with human pools on the same diversity measure.

studies.label: Human metaphor-writing experiment (L1/L2 writers x no AI / AI ideation / AI refinement)

assignment.what_was_assigned: GenAI usage condition (human-only, AI ideation, AI refinement). Writer background (L1 vs. L2) is a recruited trait set by eligibility screening, not assigned. Within the AI arms, L2 writers chose English or their native language for the AI interaction (self-selected). Scenario order was randomized within writer. The paper does not say how writers were allocated to the GenAI conditions. design_class is coded other because the allocation method is not stated: random allocation would make S1 an online_rct, and non-random allocation would make it observational context (quasi_people).
assignment.quote: The writing task followed a 2 × 3 between-subjects design, crossing writer background (L1 vs. L2) with GenAI usage (human-only vs. AI ideation vs. AI refinement).
assignment.locator: p. 17, Materials and Methods, Writing task and materials; pp. 4-5 ('participants generated metaphors in one of three conditions'). In the whole document, 'random' refers only to scenario order (p. 17), evaluator presentation order (p. 16), random intercepts (p. 19), and the LLM-judge sample (p. 27).

arms.name: Human-only (No AI)
arms.description: Writers wrote metaphors and explanations on their own, in English, with no GenAI assistance provided or allowed. JavaScript checks flagged tab or window switching: the first switch triggered a warning and a second ended the session (24 sessions terminated, p. 17).

arms.name: AI ideation
arms.description: Before composing each metaphor, writers received five GPT-4o (gpt-4o-2024-08-06) candidate metaphors, each with a short explanation, and could adopt, adapt, or ignore them and request regeneration (p. 17). L2 writers could interact in their native language and received English translations they could edit. 23 sessions terminated for tab switching.

arms.name: AI refinement
arms.description: Writers first composed their own metaphor, then received five GPT-4o candidate explanations for it and finalized the explanation; the metaphor remained the writer's own (pp. 17-18). The L1 prompt (Fig. S7) bars metaphor suggestions; the printed L2 prompt (Fig. S8) repeats the L2 ideation instructions (see open_questions). L2 writers could interact in their native language. 18 sessions terminated for tab switching.

participants.exclusions: Sessions terminated for tab or window switching: 24 human-only and 23 AI ideation (p. 17), 18 AI refinement (p. 18). The paper does not say whether these 65 sessions are inside or outside the 644 recruited writers. Per-arm counts are not printed (preregistered target 100 per cell, p. 16). Diversity models: N writer = 644 and 2,493 metaphor observations (Tab. S1, p. 28), fewer than the 2,576 that four metaphors per writer would give; the gap is not explained. Rating models: N writer = 644, N evaluator = 351, 8,241 ratings (Tab. S2, pp. 28-29). Models restricted to the AI arms: N writer = 441 (ratings) and 440 (diversity) (Tab. S3, p. 29). 228 L2 writers were in the AI arms, 84 of whom (37%) chose their native language (p. 8, p. 18).
participants.who: Prolific writers. L1: English as sole native language, born and residing in a majority-English-speaking country (n = 318). L2: a native language other than English (n = 326; 34 languages, most commonly Arabic, Portuguese, Italian, Polish, and Spanish). Mean age 36.1 (SD 12.6, range 18-79), 49% women, 66% White; paid £3.5 for a median 20 minutes. A separate Prolific sample of 351 native-English evaluators rated the metaphors (p. 16).
participants.country: not_stated (L1 writers born and residing in a majority-English-speaking country; L2 writers' countries not stated)
participants.quote: We preregistered a target of 600 writers, 100 per cell in the 2 × 3 design, and ultimately recruited 644 writers via Prolific between March 11 and 15, 2026.

ai_tool.name_model: GPT-4o (gpt-4o-2024-08-06), with scripted system prompts (SI Figs. S5-S8)
ai_tool.how_used: AI ideation arm: before each metaphor, a chat gave five metaphor-plus-explanation suggestion pairs and continued until the writer was satisfied; writers could adopt, adapt, or ignore them and request regeneration (ideas_supplied). AI refinement arm: the writer first gave the metaphor, then received five candidate explanations; the L1 prompt prohibits the model from suggesting the metaphor (Fig. S7) (closest code: refinement). L2 writers in both AI arms chose English or their native language; 84 of 228 chose their native language and received English translations to edit before submission (p. 18). The study-level role is the one for the arm closest to free chatbot use.

task.description: Four scenarios (most boring class, most disgusting food or drink, worst movie or TV show, messiest room), presented in randomized order; for each, one creative metaphor in the fixed format 'It feels like ___. This is because ___.' Instructions emphasized novel, surprising comparisons and avoiding clichés (p. 17).
task.duration: Median completion time 20 minutes for the whole session (p. 16).

outcomes.name: Collective diversity: centroid similarity of metaphor-text embeddings
outcomes.question: across_people
outcomes.measure_detail: Cosine similarity of each metaphor's embedding (only the 'It feels like ___' text; sentence-transformers all-MiniLM-L6-v2) to the leave-one-out centroid of all other metaphors for the same scenario in the same GenAI condition. Higher = less diverse, so the sign is reversed for diversity and 'direction' below refers to diversity. Primary collective measure, chosen after registration among the preregistered collective-diversity measures (p. 20). Linear mixed model on per-metaphor scores with random intercepts for writer and scenario, treatment-coded, so the condition main effects are simple effects for L1 writers (p. 19). In the AI refinement arm the embedded metaphor text was written before the AI supplied explanations (pp. 17-18). Kernel densities in Fig. 2C-D.

diversity_detail.metric: Cosine similarity of each metaphor to the leave-one-out centroid of its condition-by-scenario pool (mean centroid similarity); higher = more homogeneous
diversity_detail.computed_over: Each metaphor against the leave-one-out centroid of 'all other metaphors written for the same scenario in the same condition' (pp. 18-19; Fig. 2 caption, p. 7: 'in the same condition and scenario'). The paper does not say whether L1 and L2 metaphors in one GenAI condition share a centroid. The Results speak of each group's pool (pp. 7-8), and the printed values do not fit one shared centroid. The pooled human AI-ideation mean is 0.457 (p. 10), equal to the L1 mean and above the L2 mean (0.457 and 0.451, p. 8), although L2 writers are 228 of the 440-441 writers in the AI arms (p. 8; Tab. S3, p. 29). In Fig. 2B both L2 subgroups (EN, Non-EN) lie below the overall L2 mean of Fig. 2A in each AI arm. Pools computed within each plotted group would explain both patterns, but the paper does not state the pooling.
diversity_detail.uncertainty: Linear mixed-effects model on per-metaphor centroid similarity with random intercepts for writer and scenario (statsmodels 0.14.6); 95% CIs and p-values in Tab. S1; Fig. 2 error bars are ± SEM
diversity_detail.notes: Tab. S1 condition main effects are L1 simple effects; no whole-sample (L1 + L2) AI effect and no L2 simple effect is printed. Within-condition L1 vs. L2 gaps (No AI Δ = 0.024, p = 0.003; AI ideation Δ = 0.006, p = 0.481; AI refinement Δ = 0.018, p = 0.032; pp. 7-8) compare a recruited trait, not GenAI conditions. Language-of-interaction comparisons among L2 writers are kept in notes. Fig. 3A and 3D also show each human condition as one pool of all its writers (figure only). Only the AI ideation pool mean (0.457, p. 10) is printed, and no test between human conditions is printed. If the Tab. S1 pools are split by writer background, these figure-only pools are the only arm-level measure across all participants, which is the measure codebook section 8 prefers for across_people.

outcomes.question: with_ai

outcomes.name: Divergent creativity rating (novelty + surprise)
outcomes.question: with_ai
outcomes.measure_detail: 351 native-English Prolific evaluators, blind to writer background and condition, rated each metaphor together with its explanation on 0-100 sliders; novelty and surprise averaged into the divergent subscale (Spearman-Brown rSB = 0.86). Each evaluator rated 24 metaphors, six per scenario, drawn equally from the three conditions. Treatment-coded mixed model with random intercepts for evaluator, writer, and scenario; condition main effects are L1 simple effects (p. 19, Tab. S2). Human ratings are the paper's chosen measure of individual creative performance (p. 20). Robustness: quantile regressions at τ = 0.1-0.9 on metaphor-level mean ratings, by writer background (Fig. S4, p. 25; text p. 13; not preregistered). The rating counts do not match this design: 351 evaluators x 24 metaphors gives 8,424 ratings, but the models hold 8,241 (Tab. S2, p. 29), and the AI-arm model holds 5,638 (Tab. S3, p. 29), more than the 5,616 (351 x 16) that equal draws allow. The paper explains neither gap.

Text p. 12: L1 b = 4.753, p < 0.001; L2 b = 0.834, p = 0.548. Quantile regressions (p. 13): L1 β = +7.5, p < 0.001 at τ = 0.1 vs. β = +4.5, p = 0.003 at τ = 0.9; L2 significant only at τ ≤ 0.2. outcomes.name: LLM-judge creativity score (Bradley-Terry, z within rater)
outcomes.question: with_ai
outcomes.measure_detail: Preregistered automated LLM-based scoring of individual creative performance that the paper set aside after validation because the scorers ranked inconsistently and favored LLM-generated content (p. 20). Three LLM judges (GPT-4o mini, Claude Sonnet 4, Qwen3-8B) repeatedly ranked randomly sampled metaphors; Bradley-Terry scores standardized within rater and compared by condition with the blinded human panel. Rank agreement with the human panel: heatmap cells 0.32 (GPT-4o mini), 0.37 (Claude Sonnet 4), 0.30 (Qwen3-8B), while the caption prints ρ = 0.31–0.38; the judges agree with one another at ρ = 0.68–0.87. n = 2,235 metaphors (Fig. S10 caption). Figure only.

contrasts.reported: Figure only (z within rater, mean ± SEM); no numbers or test printed. All three LLM judges score AI ideation above No AI, as does the human panel. Caption: 'two of the three LLM judges (GPT-4o mini, Qwen3-8B) sharply over-reward AI-ideation metaphors'.

contrasts.reported: Figure only; no numbers or test printed. All three LLM judges, Claude Sonnet 4 included, score AI refinement below No AI, while the human panel scores it above No AI. arms.name: Human pool, No AI (S1 human-only)
arms.description: Metaphors written by the S1 writers without AI.

arms.name: Human pools, AI ideation and AI refinement (S1 AI arms)
arms.description: Metaphors written by the S1 writers with GPT-4o help. The AI ideation pool, the least diverse human pool, is the comparison pool for the paper's printed differences.

arms.name: LLM-simulated pools
arms.description: Persona-conditioned metaphors from GPT-4o mini (gpt-4o-mini-2024-07-18), Claude Sonnet 4.6, and Qwen3.5-27b at the provider default temperature (1.0) for the main comparison; a native-language pipeline for personas of L2 writers who had used their native language; and a temperature sweep from 0.5 to 2.0 for GPT-4o mini and Qwen 3.5 (Claude Sonnet 4.6 only up to 1.0).

participants.quote: For every writer in all three conditions, we constructed a persona prompt from their background questionnaire

ai_tool.how_used: Models write the metaphors themselves from persona prompts (sample prompt in Fig. S2, pp. 23-24); no human receives AI help in the simulated pools.

task.description: Same four metaphor scenarios and two-part format as S1.

outcomes.name: Collective diversity of simulated vs. human metaphor pools (centroid similarity)

eligibility.reason: S1 is a preregistered 2 x 3 between-subjects online experiment on Prolific in which writers worked in one of three GenAI conditions (no AI, AI ideation, AI refinement). The document never states how writers were allocated to the conditions: 'random' refers only to scenario order, evaluator order, random intercepts, and the LLM-judge sample. Criterion 1 is therefore unclear, and design_class is coded other until the allocation is known. Nothing in the text says that writers chose their condition. Random allocation would make S1 an online_rct and the paper core; non-random allocation would make S1 observational context. 644 writers are analyzed (N writer = 644 in Tab. S1, p. 28, and Tab. S2, p. 29), far above 50, though per-arm counts are not printed. The outcomes are embedding-based diversity and blinded human ratings scored on the submitted metaphors, produced with AI available in the AI arms. Writer background is recruited and the language of AI interaction was self-chosen, so those comparisons are not randomized. S2 (LLM personas vs. human pools) is ai_vs_human context evidence.

one_line_finding: AI ideation made metaphors more alike than writing without AI (centroid similarity, L1 simple effect b = 0.036, 95% CI 0.017 to 0.056, Tab. S1 p. 28; L2 means 0.398 vs. 0.451, pp. 7-8) while AI refinement did not (L1 b = 0.007, p = 0.516), and AI ideation raised L1 writers' blind divergent ratings (b = 4.75, 95% CI 2.00 to 7.50, Tab. S2 p. 28) but not L2 writers' (b = 0.834, p = 0.548, p. 12).
open_questions: Random assignment of writers to the GenAI conditions is not stated anywhere in the document, so design_class is coded other and criterion 1 is unclear. Check the preregistration (https://tinyurl.com/DiverseCreativity) or the OSF materials and code; if they are silent, ask the authors.

Per-arm writer counts are not printed (target 100 per cell, p. 16). The document gives only L1 = 318, L2 = 326, 228 L2 writers in the AI arms (p. 18), and N writer = 441 (rating model) and 440 (diversity model) in the AI-arm models (Tab. S3, p. 29). The one-writer gap between those two models is not explained.

Whether the 65 tab-switch terminations (24, 23, 18; pp. 17-18) are inside or outside the 644 recruited writers is not stated, and Tab. S1 has 2,493 metaphor observations where 644 writers with four metaphors each would give 2,576; the gap is not explained.

Fig. S8, labeled the AI refinement prompt for L2 participants (pp. 26-27), prints the L2 ideation instructions of Fig. S6 ('provide 5 suggestion pairs of the first and second blanks'), not the ban on metaphor suggestions in Fig. S7. Either the SI has a copy error or L2 writers in AI refinement also received metaphor suggestions.

The headline diversity coefficients (b = 0.036 and b = 0.007, p. 7) are simple effects for L1 writers under treatment coding (p. 19), though the text presents them as general effects of each workflow; no whole-sample (L1 + L2) AI effect is printed.

On p. 12 the L2 refinement effects printed as 'divergent: b = -3.138, p = 0.124; convergent: b = -1.756, p = 0.296' equal the AI refinement × L2 interaction terms in Tab. S2, not L2 simple effects; later on p. 12 the L2 convergent refinement effect is b = 1.485, p = 0.219. The L2 divergent refinement simple effect is not printed.

Whether L1 and L2 metaphors share a centroid in the S1 diversity analyses is not stated. The pooled AI-ideation mean of 0.457 (p. 10) and the Fig. 2B subgroup means do not fit one shared centroid. If the pools are split by writer background, the Tab. S1 effects compare within-background pools, and the only arm-level measure across all participants is figure-only (Fig. 3A, 3D).

How mean pairwise cosine distance, semantic distance to prompt, and TTR (Fig. S9) were computed is not stated: embedding model, text embedded, pooling, and unit. The units of S1-O3 to S1-O5 and the construct codes of S1-O4 (novelty) and S1-O5 (other) are therefore provisional.

The Fig. S10A heatmap gives LLM-human rank agreement of 0.30-0.37, while the caption says 0.31-0.38. In Fig. S10B all three LLM judges place AI refinement below No AI, though the caption names only GPT-4o mini and Qwen3-8B.

Rating standard errors come from a rating-level mixed model (random intercepts for evaluator, writer, scenario) and diversity standard errors from a metaphor-level model (random intercepts for writer and scenario); no participant-level SDs are printed.

Rating counts do not match the stated evaluator design: 351 x 24 = 8,424 ratings, but the rating models hold 8,241 (Tab. S2, p. 29), and the AI-arm model holds 5,638 (Tab. S3, p. 29), more than the 5,616 that equal draws from the three conditions allow.

challenge_resolution.problem: S1-O1 computed_over says L1 and L2 metaphors in one condition share a centroid, but the paper never says so and the printed means do not fit a shared centroid; S1-O2 glosses the pool as 'same GenAI condition'.
challenge_resolution.what_changed: S1-O1 and S1-O2 computed_over now quote the paper ('same scenario in the same condition') and say that the pooling by writer background is not stated. S1-O1 records the evidence against one shared centroid. The pooled human AI-ideation mean is 0.457 (p. 10), equal to the L1 mean and above the L2 mean (0.457 and 0.451, p. 8). With one shared centroid it would be a weighted average of the two. The p. 8 shares (84 of 228 L2 writers; 39 percent in AI ideation, 34 percent in AI refinement) fit only 109 to 148 L2 writers in AI ideation, so even if all 213 AI-arm L1 writers were in that arm the average is at most 0.4555, below the 0.4565 that prints as 0.457. Fig. 3D plots the No AI pool near 0.414, above the 0.410 that the printed No AI means (0.421 and 0.398, p. 7) give for its derived 98 L2 and about 105 L1 writers. In Fig. 2B both L2 subgroups lie below the overall L2 mean of Fig. 2A in each AI arm, which one set of per-metaphor scores cannot produce. S1-O1 diversity_detail.notes now names the figure-only arm-level pools (Fig. 3A, 3D), and open_questions adds the pooling question.

open_items.item: Allocation of writers to the GenAI conditions (open question 1). The paper calls S1 a preregistered 2 x 3 between-subjects design but never says how writers were allocated to human-only, AI ideation, or AI refinement. If allocation was random, S1 is an online_rct and the paper enters the core. If it was not, S1 is observational context. The preregistration (https://tinyurl.com/DiverseCreativity) and the OSF materials and code should show the allocation rule; if they do not, the authors.
Writers per arm (open question 2), including the 441 vs. 440 writers in the two AI-arm models. Criterion 2 holds on the 644 writers analyzed. The counts matter for n_treatment and n_control.
Whether the 65 tab-switch terminations are inside the 644, and why Tab. S1 holds 2,493 metaphors rather than 2,576 (open question 3). Criterion 2 holds either way, because 644 writers are analyzed.

Fig. S8 prints the L2 ideation instructions as the L2 refinement prompt (open question 4). Either way, L2 refinement writers received GPT-4o help, so the AI-versus-no-AI contrast is unchanged. The prompt matters for describing the refinement arm.
No whole-sample (L1 + L2) AI effect on diversity or ratings is printed; the table coefficients are L1 simple effects (open question 5). This decides which statistic extraction uses, not eligibility.
The L2 refinement effects printed on p. 12 equal the Tab. S2 interaction terms, and the L2 divergent refinement simple effect is not printed (open question 6).

Whether L1 and L2 metaphors share a centroid in the S1 diversity analyses (open question 7). The printed means do not fit one shared centroid. If the pools are split by background, the arm-level measure across all participants is figure-only (Fig. 3A, 3D). Criterion 3 holds either way.
S1-O3 unit, the one unresolved reconciliation difference: mean pairwise cosine distance could be analyzed per output, per pair, or per pool. The provisional value is output.

Computation of the other Fig. S9 measures (open question 8): embedding model, text embedded, pooling, and unit. It leaves the S1-O4 construct (novelty) and the S1-O5 coding (other, with_ai, output) provisional.

Fig. S10A heatmap (0.30-0.37) vs. caption (0.31-0.38), and the caption names two LLM judges where Fig. S10B shows all three below No AI under AI refinement (open question 9). S1-O8 is a secondary, figure-only outcome that the paper set aside, and the form records both readings.
Standard errors come from rating-level and metaphor-level mixed models, and no participant-level SDs are printed (open question 10). Standardized effects need the posted data.

Rating counts do not match the evaluator design (open question 11): 8,241 ratings instead of 8,424, and 5,638 in the AI-arm model, above the 5,616 that equal draws allow. The ratings are units, not people, so criterion 2 is unaffected.
